accords-latins.title: Fretting hand: Latin chords
accords-latins.description: Richer and richer chord changes, always with a simple rhythm so all your attention goes to your fretting hand.

accords-01-am-f.title: Am ↔ F: just one finger to add
accords-01-am-f.description: The easiest change there is: Am takes one finger (G string, fret 2), and F keeps that finger and adds one more (E string, fret 1). Perfect for learning NOT to lift your fingers for nothing.
accords-01-am-f.goal: Change without ever lifting the finger on the G string, 2 loops at 80 bpm.
tips: The finger on the G string stays glued down: it's your "pivot".
Place the 2nd finger during beat 4, not after the 1.
Bolero is slow: make the most of it and let each chord ring all the way through.

accords-02-bolero.title: Bolero: C – Am – F – G7
accords-02-bolero.description: The progression behind a thousand romantic songs, over the slow bolero rhythm. The "down, down-up, down, down-up" pattern is soft and steady: let the chords breathe.
accords-02-bolero.goal: All 4 chords back to back with no gaps, 2 loops at 80 bpm.
tips: C → Am: one finger leaves, another arrives. Am → F: one finger is added. F → G7: the shape shifts over.
Play more gently than for cumbia: bolero is sung close to the ear.
Listen to the bongos rolling in eighth notes: they give you the speed of your strumming hand.

accords-03-demi-mesure.title: Two chords per bar
accords-03-demi-mesure.description: The same progression, but twice as tight: a new chord every two beats. The rhythm is simplified (one strum per beat) so your fretting hand has time to keep up.
accords-03-demi-mesure.goal: All 4 changes per bar, 2 loops at 85 bpm.
tips: You only get 2 beats per chord: start the change as early as beat 2.
Keep your fingers close to the strings: the less they wander, the faster you are.
Go back to "Bolero: C – Am – F – G7" if one change won't come.

accords-04-cycle-septiemes.title: The cycle of sevenths: A7 – D7 – G7 – C
accords-04-cycle-septiemes.description: Each seventh chord "calls" the next one, all the way to the C that resolves everything. It's the king of progressions in Cuban music (and jazz). Listen to the tension of each 7th and the relief of the C.
accords-04-cycle-septiemes.goal: The full cycle, 2 loops at 95 bpm.
tips: A7: just one finger (C string, fret 1). D7: a barre or three fingers on fret 2. G7: the triangle shape. C: one finger.
D7 → G7: the finger on the C string (fret 2) stays put — it's your anchor point.
Listen: each 7th sounds "suspended", and the final C settles everything. Once you can hear it, you know where you are without looking at the screen.

accords-05-bossa-251.title: Jazzy chords in bossa: Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7
accords-05-bossa-251.description: The famous "II – V – I" with that unmistakably Brazilian sound, using bossa's thumb-and-fingers technique. The shapes sit close to each other: your hand glides more than it jumps.
accords-05-bossa-251.goal: A steady thumb and ringing chords, 2 loops at 85 bpm.
tips: Dm7 → G7: two fingers stay put (C string fret 2, E string fret 1); only the ones on the G and A strings move.
Cmaj7: just one finger (A string, fret 2) — enjoy it for 2 bars.
Do "Bossa nova: thumb and fingers" first if the pattern isn't automatic yet.
